newsitem.title: UK: UK pensions watchdog seeks improved regulation.
newsitem.headline: UK pensions watchdog seeks improved regulation.

text.p: The chairman of Britain's Personal Investment Authority called on consumers and companies on Wednesday to suggest ways of improving the way the UK retail investment sector is regulated.
Joe Palmer told an insurance industry conference in London of the Evolution Project -- a plan to review the workings of the PIA two years after its formation.
"It is an open invitation to consumers and customers alike to contribute to improving the way in which we regulate the retail investment sector," said Palmer.
The PIA was set up in July 1994 after a wave of scandals about the mis-selling of pensions and other investment products.

"PIA is emphatically not seeking to revolutionise its current approach to regulation, but it is attempting to improve the regulatory effectiveness and to see whether there are areas where the PIA's requirements have become unduly complicated or prescriptive," he added.
Palmer said it was time to address issues such as whether investors are given too much information and the impact of new technology.

"We are conscious of the risk of information overload for the many investors who are infrequent purchasers in this market. The PIA wishes to explore...whether it is possible to cut the paper mountain by allowing firms to incorporate key informstion into product brochures," Palmer said.
He added that he intends to examine whther investors should be licensed to assure investors of their competence.
Palmer also asked for views on controversial "execution only" business, where investment products are sold direct to the consumer without any intermediary advice.

"It has been suggested that that it is inappropriate for products such as pensions to be sold without advice. PIA does not accept this view. Provided an investor is given all relevant information on a particular product, it is a matter of individual choice if the investor wants to buy it," he said.
Palmer said it would be excessively interventionist to prohibit customers as it would restrict competition.
"However we are seeking views as to whether direct offer advertisements might be required to give a clear and unambiguous warning to investors that no advice is being given," he said.
"Similarly, should an oral warning to the same effect be required where a firm has a telephone helpline providing information, but not advice, about a product?" he said.
